claim: Exercise promotes the formation of intracellular junctions in skeletal muscle between stacks of sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) cisternae and extensions of transverse-tubules (TT).
source: Exercise promotes the formation of intracellular junctions in skeletal muscle between stacks of sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) cisternae and extensions of transverse-tubules (TT) that increase co-localization of proteins required for store-operated Ca2+ entry (SOCE).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data from electron microscopy showing SR-stacks and TT extensions, as well as immunofluorescence data showing increased STIM1-Orai1 co-localization.

claim: Exercise-induced junctions increase co-localization of proteins required for store-operated Ca2+ entry (SOCE).
source: Exercise promotes the formation of intracellular junctions in skeletal muscle between stacks of sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) cisternae and extensions of transverse-tubules (TT) that increase co-localization of proteins required for store-operated Ca2+ entry (SOCE).
evidence: This is supported by previous immunofluorescence and immunogold studies cited in the manuscript showing increased STIM1-Orai1 co-localization after exercise.

claim: SOCE is increased after exercise in parallel with the time course of TT association with SR-stacks.
source: Here, we report that SOCE, peak Ca2+ transient amplitude and muscle force production during repetitive stimulation are increased after exercise in parallel with the time course of TT association with SR-stacks.
evidence: This is supported by Mn2+ quench data showing increased SOCE activity and EM data showing TT-SR contact formation with similar time courses.

claim: Peak Ca2+ transient amplitude during repetitive stimulation is increased after exercise in parallel with the time course of TT association with SR-stacks.
source: Here, we report that SOCE, peak Ca2+ transient amplitude and muscle force production during repetitive stimulation are increased after exercise in parallel with the time course of TT association with SR-stacks.
evidence: This is supported by mag-fluo-4 Ca2+ transient measurements during repetitive stimulation showing increased peak amplitude after exercise.

claim: Muscle force production during repetitive stimulation is increased after exercise in parallel with the time course of TT association with SR-stacks.
source: Here, we report that SOCE, peak Ca2+ transient amplitude and muscle force production during repetitive stimulation are increased after exercise in parallel with the time course of TT association with SR-stacks.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo muscle contractility measurements showing increased force maintenance during repetitive stimulation after exercise.

claim: Exercise activates constitutive Ca2+ entry coincident with a modest decrease in total releasable Ca2+ store content.
source: Unexpectedly, exercise also activated constitutive Ca2+ entry coincident with a modest decrease in total releasable Ca2+ store content.
evidence: This is supported by Mn2+ quench measurements in non-depleted fibers and fura-FF measurements of total Ca2+ store content.

claim: The decrease in releasable Ca2+ store content observed after exercise was reversed by repetitive high-frequency stimulation.
source: Importantly, this decrease in releasable Ca2+ store content observed after exercise was reversed by repetitive high-frequency stimulation, consistent with enhanced SOCE.
evidence: This is supported by fura-FF measurements showing increased total Ca2+ store content after 10 stimulus trains in fibers from exercised mice.

claim: The functional benefits of exercise on SOCE, constitutive Ca2+ entry and muscle force production were lost in mice with muscle-specific loss of Orai1 function.
source: The functional benefits of exercise on SOCE, constitutive Ca2+ entry and muscle force production were lost in mice with muscle-specific loss of Orai1 function.
evidence: This is supported by experiments in iOrai1 KO and dnOrai1 mice showing no increase in SOCE or force production after exercise.

claim: TT association with SR-stacks enhances Orai1-dependent SOCE to optimize Ca2+ dynamics and muscle contractile function during acute exercise.
source: These results indicate that TT association with SR-stacks enhances Orai1-dependent SOCE to optimize Ca2+ dynamics and muscle contractile function during acute exercise.
evidence: This is an integrative conclusion based on the combined structural and functional data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SOCE is mediated by the coupling between STIM1 in the ER membrane and Orai1 channels in the plasma membrane.
source: Store-operated Ca2+ entry (SOCE), a Ca2+ entry mechanism activated by depletion of intracellular stores, is mediated by the coupling between stromal interacting molecule-1 (STIM1), a luminal Ca2+ sensor protein in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane (Roos et al., 2005), and Ca2+-permeable Orai1 channels in the plasma membrane (Feske et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational studies identifying STIM1 and Orai1 as key SOCE components.

claim: In skeletal muscle, SOCE is coordinated by a functional interaction between STIM1 in the SR and Orai1 in the TT.
source: In skeletal muscle, SOCE is similarly coordinated by a functional interaction between STIM1 in the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) and Orai1 in the transverse tubule (TT) (Kurebayashi and Ogawa, 2001; Lyfenko and Dirksen, 2008; Stiber et al., 2008), specialized invaginations of the surface membrane that propagate action potentials to trigger SR Ca2+ release during excitation-contraction (EC) coupling.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies demonstrating STIM1-Orai1 coupling in skeletal muscle.

claim: SOCE has been proposed to promote myoblast fusion/differentiation and muscle development.
source: While the precise physiological role(s) of SOCE in muscle remains incompletely defined, SOCE has been proposed to promote myoblast fusion/differentiation (Darbellay et al., 2009) and muscle development (Kurebayashi and Ogawa, 2001; Wei-Lapierre et al., 2013; Carrell et al., 2016)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies investigating SOCE roles in muscle development.

claim: SOCE has been proposed to reduce fatigue during periods of prolonged stimulation.
source: SOCE has been proposed to promote myoblast fusion/differentiation (Darbellay et al., 2009) and muscle development (Kurebayashi and Ogawa, 2001; Wei-Lapierre et al., 2013; Carrell et al., 2016), reduce fatigue during periods of prolonged stimulation (Wei-Lapierre et al., 2013; Carrell et al., 2016; Pan et al., 2002; Boncompagni et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing SOCE's role in reducing muscle fatigue.

claim: SOCE serves as a counter-flux to Ca2+ loss across the TT system during EC coupling.
source: SOCE has been proposed to promote myoblast fusion/differentiation (Darbellay et al., 2009) and muscle development (Kurebayashi and Ogawa, 2001; Wei-Lapierre et al., 2013; Carrell et al., 2016), reduce fatigue during periods of prolonged stimulation (Wei-Lapierre et al., 2013; Carrell et al., 2016; Pan et al., 2002; Boncompagni et al., 2017), as well as serve as a counter-flux to Ca2+ loss across the TT system during EC coupling (Koenig et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a study proposing this mechanism.

claim: Mutations in the genes that encode STIM1 and Orai1 underlie an array of disorders with clinical myopathy as central defining component.
source: Importantly, mutations in the genes that encode STIM1 and Orai1 underlie an array of disorders with clinical myopathy as central deﬁning component.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of STIM1 and Orai1 mutations causing muscle disease.

claim: SOCE dysfunction contributes to the pathogenesis of several muscle disorders.
source: SOCE dysfunction also contributes to the pathogenesis of several other muscle disorders (Michelucci et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article on SOCE in muscle disease.

claim: SOCE plays an important role in both normal muscle development/function and muscle disease.
source: Thus, SOCE plays an important role in both normal muscle development/function and muscle disease.
evidence: This is an inference based on the preceding discussion of SOCE's roles in muscle.

claim: In resting mammalian skeletal muscle, STIM1 proteins are found throughout the I band of the sarcomere.
source: In resting mammalian skeletal muscle, STIM1 proteins are found throughout the I band of the sarcomere (Stiber et al., 2008; Wei-Lapierre et al., 2013; Boncompagni et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing STIM1 localization in muscle.

claim: Orai1 channels at rest are found almost exclusively at the A-I band junction, in accordance with their localization within the TT membrane of the triad.
source: On the other hand, Orai1 channels at rest are found almost exclusively at the A-I band junction, in accordance with their localization within the TT membrane of the triad (Wei-Lapierre et al., 2013; Boncompagni et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies showing Orai1 localization in muscle.

claim: A modest degree of STIM1-Orai1 co-localization at the A-I band junction at rest has been suggested to explain the uniquely rapid activation of SOCE (<1 s) observed in skeletal muscle.
source: A modest degree of STIM1-Orai1 co-localization at the A-I band junction at rest has been suggested to explain in part the uniquely rapid activation of SOCE (<1 s) observed in skeletal muscle (Koenig et al., 2018; Launikonis and Ríos, 2007; Edwards et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on rapid SOCE activation in muscle.

claim: Acute treadmill exercise drives a significant reorganization of the sarcotubular membranes in the I band of EDL fibers that involves remodeling of the SR into stacks of flat cisternae.
source: However, STIM1 and Orai1 localization in muscle is not static, as acute treadmill exercise drives a significant reorganization of the sarcotubular membranes in the I band of extensor digitorum longus (EDL) fibers of wild type (WT) mice that involves: i) remodeling of the SR into stacks of flat cisternae
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors showing SR remodeling after exercise.

claim: Acute treadmill exercise drives elongation of the TT into the I band.
source: However, STIM1 and Orai1 localization in muscle is not static, as acute treadmill exercise drives a significant reorganization of the sarcotubular membranes in the I band of extensor digitorum longus (EDL) fibers of wild type (WT) mice that involves: i) remodeling of the SR into stacks of flat cisternae; ii) elongation of the TT into the I band
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors showing TT elongation after exercise.

claim: Acute treadmill exercise drives increased co-localization of Orai1 with STIM1 in the I band.
source: However, STIM1 and Orai1 localization in muscle is not static, as acute treadmill exercise drives a significant reorganization of the sarcotubular membranes in the I band of extensor digitorum longus (EDL) fibers of wild type (WT) mice that involves: i) remodeling of the SR into stacks of flat cisternae; ii) elongation of the TT into the I band; and iii) increased co-localization of Orai1 with STIM1 in the I band (Boncompagni et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors showing increased STIM1-Orai1 co-localization after exercise.

claim: Exercise-induced remodeling leads to the formation of new SR-TT contacts that are structurally distinct from triad junctions in that they are oriented longitudinally at the I band.
source: This exercise-induced remodeling leads to the formation of new SR-TT contacts that are structurally distinct from triad junctions in that they are oriented longitudinally at the I band (while triads are transversally oriented at the A-I band junction)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors describing the structural features of these junctions.

claim: Exercise-induced SR-TT contacts display a junctional gap of only 7–8 nm while triads exhibit a 12 nm junctional gap.
source: This exercise-induced remodeling leads to the formation of new SR-TT contacts that are structurally distinct from triad junctions in that they are oriented longitudinally at the I band (while triads are transversally oriented at the A-I band junction) and display a junctional gap of only 7–8 nm (while triads exhibit a 12 nm junctional gap) (Boncompagni et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors measuring junctional gap widths.

claim: The formation of SR-TT junctions following acute exercise correlates with an increased resistance to EDL muscle contractile decline during repetitive stimulation in presence of extracellular Ca2+.
source: Importantly, the formation of these junctions following acute exercise correlates with an increased resistance to EDL muscle contractile decline during repetitive stimulation in presence of extracellular Ca2+, but not under conditions that reduce SOCE (0 Ca2, BTP-2, 2-APB) (Boncompagni et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors showing this correlation.

claim: The formation of SR-TT junctions following acute exercise does not correlate with increased resistance to contractile decline under conditions that reduce SOCE (0 Ca2+, BTP-2, 2-APB).
source: Importantly, the formation of these junctions following acute exercise correlates with an increased resistance to EDL muscle contractile decline during repetitive stimulation in presence of extracellular Ca2+, but not under conditions that reduce SOCE (0 Ca2, BTP-2, 2-APB) (Boncompagni et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study by the authors showing this lack of correlation under SOCE-inhibiting conditions.

claim: SR-TT junctions formed within the I band following acute exercise were suggested to function as Calcium Entry Units (CEUs).
source: As the formation of the SR-TT junctions within the I band following acute exercise are coincident with enhanced STIM1-Orai1 co-localization and force production during sustained activity, these structural elements were suggested to function as Calcium Entry Units (CEUs).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between structural changes and functional outcomes.

claim: The percentage of EDL muscle fibers with SR-stacks in the I band was significantly increased shortly after exercise (<1 hr) compared to non-exercised control mice.
source: Shortly after exercise (<1 hr), the percentage of muscle fibers with SR-stacks in the I band (Figure 1E), the number of stacks/100 µm2 (Figure 1F), and SR-stack length (Figure 1G) were all significantly increased compared to that of non-exercised control mice.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative EM analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The number of SR-stacks/100 µm2 in EDL muscle fibers was significantly increased shortly after exercise (<1 hr) compared to non-exercised control mice.
source: Shortly after exercise (<1 hr), the percentage of muscle fibers with SR-stacks in the I band (Figure 1E), the number of stacks/100 µm2 (Figure 1F), and SR-stack length (Figure 1G) were all significantly increased compared to that of non-exercised control mice.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative EM analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: SR-stack length in EDL muscle fibers was significantly increased shortly after exercise (<1 hr) compared to non-exercised control mice.
source: Shortly after exercise (<1 hr), the percentage of muscle fibers with SR-stacks in the I band (Figure 1E), the number of stacks/100 µm2 (Figure 1F), and SR-stack length (Figure 1G) were all significantly increased compared to that of non-exercised control mice.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative EM analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The percentage of fibers with SR-stacks at the I band and the number of SR stacks/100 µm2 further increased 6 hr after exercise.
source: The percentage of fibers with SR-stacks at the I band and the number of SR stacks/100 µm2 further increased 6 hr after exercise.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative EM analysis shown in Figures 1E and 1F.

claim: All three SR-stack parameters decreased to values closer to that of fibers from non-exercised control mice 24 hr after exercise.
source: All three parameters decreased to values closer to that of fibers from non-exercised control mice 24 hr after exercise.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative EM analysis shown in Figures 1E-G.

claim: A similar time course of SR-stack formation and disassembly was observed in FDB muscle fibers.
source: A similar time course was also observed in FDB muscle fibers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative EM analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The TT/SR contact length within the I band region of the sarcomere increased 5-fold < 1 hr after exercise.
source: The results indicate that the TT/SR contact length within the I band region of the sarcomere increased 5-fold < 1 hr after exercise and then returned to levels not significantly different from control both 6 and 24 hr after exercise (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative EM analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: TT/SR contact length returned to levels not significantly different from control both 6 and 24 hr after exercise.
source: The results indicate that the TT/SR contact length within the I band region of the sarcomere increased 5-fold < 1 hr after exercise and then returned to levels not significantly different from control both 6 and 24 hr after exercise (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative EM analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The increase in TT/SR contact length after exercise is consistent with increased Orai1-STIM1 co-localization within the I band <1 hr after exercise.
source: The increase in TT/SR contact length after exercise is consistent with our prior demonstration (using immunofluorescence and immuno-gold electron microscopy) of increased Orai1-STIM1 co-localization within the I band <1 hr after exercise (Boncompagni et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on consistency with previous immunofluorescence and immuno-gold EM data.

claim: Total TT length/100 µm2 was significantly increased in EDL muscle fibers from mice < 1 hr after exercise compared to control samples.
source: In addition, total TT length/100 µm2 was also significantly increased in EDL muscle fibers from mice < 1 hr after exercise (Figure 2B and F) compared to that of control samples (Figure 2A and F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative EM analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Increased extensions of the TT network within the I band observed <1 hr after exercise were not different from control 6 and 24 hr after exercise.
source: Importantly, in contrast to that observed for SR-stacks (Figure 1), increased extensions of the TT network (and TT/SR contact length) within the I band, observed <1 hr after exercise, were not different from control 6 and 24 hr after exercise (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative EM analysis shown in Figures 2E and 2F.

claim: A transient increase in total TT length/100 µm2 and a more prolonged increase in SR stacks at the I band after exercise was observed in FDB muscle fibers.
source: A transient increase in total TT length/100 µm2 and with a more prolonged increase in SR stacks at the I band after exercise was also observed in FDB muscle fibers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative EM analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The maximum rate of Mn2+ quench was significantly increased (~70%) in FDB fibers isolated from mice < 1 hr after treadmill exercise compared to control mice following store depletion.
source: Importantly, compared to that of control mice, the maximum rate of Mn2+ quench was significantly increased (~70%) in FDB fibers isolated from mice < 1 hr after treadmill exercise (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by Mn2+ quench measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The maximum rate of Mn2+ quench was not different from that of control mice following 6 and 24 hr of recovery.
source: The maximum rate of Mn2+ quench was not different from that of control mice following 6 and 24 hr of recovery.
evidence: This is supported by Mn2+ quench measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: An analysis of the frequency distribution of maximal rate of Mn2+ quench in SR depleted fibers showed a shift toward larger rates of quench in fibers from mice < 1 hr after exercise.
source: An analysis of the frequency distribution of maximal rate of Mn2+ quench in SR depleted fibers showed a shift toward larger rates of quench in fibers from mice < 1 hr after exercise, but not in fibers isolated at 6 and 24 hr of recovery (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by frequency histogram analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Fura-2 quench did not occur upon addition of Mn2+ to fibers from non-exercised mice in the absence of pharmacological store depletion.
source: While fura-2 quench did not occur upon addition of Mn2+ to fibers from non-exercised mice, a marked increase in quench rate was observed in fibers from mice < 1 hr after exercise (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by Mn2+ quench measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A marked increase in Mn2+ quench rate was observed in fibers from mice < 1 hr after exercise in the absence of pharmacological store depletion.
source: While fura-2 quench did not occur upon addition of Mn2+ to fibers from non-exercised mice, a marked increase in quench rate was observed in fibers from mice < 1 hr after exercise (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by Mn2+ quench measurements shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The maximum rate of Mn2+ quench in the absence of pharmacological store depletion was significantly increased at <1 hr after exercise.
source: Consistent with the morphological observations in TT length (Figure 2), the maximum rate of Mn2+ quench in the absence of pharmacological store depletion was significantly increased at <1 hr after exercise, reduced at 6 hr, but essentially undetectable at 24 hr after exercise (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by Mn2+ quench measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The maximum rate of Mn2+ quench in the absence of pharmacological store depletion was reduced at 6 hr after exercise.
source: Consistent with the morphological observations in TT length (Figure 2), the maximum rate of Mn2+ quench in the absence of pharmacological store depletion was significantly increased at <1 hr after exercise, reduced at 6 hr, but essentially undetectable at 24 hr after exercise (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by Mn2+ quench measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The maximum rate of Mn2+ quench in the absence of pharmacological store depletion was essentially undetectable at 24 hr after exercise.
source: Consistent with the morphological observations in TT length (Figure 2), the maximum rate of Mn2+ quench in the absence of pharmacological store depletion was significantly increased at <1 hr after exercise, reduced at 6 hr, but essentially undetectable at 24 hr after exercise (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by Mn2+ quench measurements shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A shift toward larger Mn2+ quench rates was observed in fibers isolated from mice < 1 hr after exercise in the absence of pharmacological store depletion.
source: As a result, a shift toward larger Mn2+ quench rates was observed in fibers isolated from mice < 1 hr after exercise (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by frequency histogram analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Mn2+ quench in SR Ca2+ replete fibers from mice < 1 hr after exercise was rapidly blocked by 10 μM BTP-2.
source: Consistent with the Mn2+ quench observed in SR Ca2+ replete fibers from mice < 1 hr after exercise being mediated by Orai1 channels, Mn2+ quench in these fibers was rapidly blocked by an inhibitor of Orai1-dependent SOCE (10 μM BTP-2; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Mn2+ quench measurements with BTP-2 shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was no significant difference between the four groups in peak Ca2+ transient amplitude elicited during the 1st stimulus train.
source: Representative traces showed no significant difference between the four groups in peak Ca2+ transient amplitude elicited during the 1st stimulus train (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by mag-fluo-4 Ca2+ transient measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In FDB fibers from control mice, both absolute and relative peak Ca2+ transient amplitude exhibited a steady modest decline from the first to last stimulation train, with an average decrease of ~30% over the 40 stimuli.
source: In FDB ﬁbers from control mice, both absolute (Figure 5B) and relative (Figure 5C) peak Ca2+ transient amplitude exhibited a steady modest decline from the ﬁrst to last stimulation train, with an average decrease of ~30% over the 40 stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by mag-fluo-4 Ca2+ transient measurements shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: Fibers isolated from mice < 1 hr after exercise displayed a significant increase in both absolute and relative peak Ca2+ transient amplitude for all trains between stimuli 7–21.
source: On the other hand, fibers isolated from mice < 1 hr after exercise displayed a significant increase in both absolute and relative peak Ca2+ transient amplitude for all trains between stimuli 7–21 (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by mag-fluo-4 Ca2+ transient measurements shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: Peak Ca2+ transient amplitude elicited in fibers isolated from mice either 6 or 24 hr after exercise were not significantly different from control.
source: Finally, peak Ca2+ transient amplitude elicited in fibers isolated from mice either 6 or 24 hr after exercise, were not significantly different from control.
evidence: This is supported by mag-fluo-4 Ca2+ transient measurements shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: Resting total Ca2+ store content was significantly reduced (~25%) in fibers obtained from mice < 1 hr after exercise compared to fibers from control mice.
source: The results indicate that compared to fibers from control mice, resting total Ca2+ store content was significantly reduced (~25%) in fibers obtained from mice < 1 hr after exercise (Figure 5D)
evidence: This is supported by fura-FF measurements of total Ca2+ store content shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Total Ca2+ store content was not different from control in fibers isolated from mice 6 and 24 hr after exercise.
source: The results indicate that compared to fibers from control mice, resting total Ca2+ store content was significantly reduced (~25%) in fibers obtained from mice < 1 hr after exercise (Figure 5D), but not in fibers isolated from mice 6 and 24 hr after exercise (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by fura-FF measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: A significant increase in resting myoplasmic Ca2+ concentration was observed only in fibers < 1 hr after exercise.
source: Consistent with the increase in constitutive SOCE observed <1 hr after exercise (Figure 4B), a significant increase in resting myoplasmic Ca2+ concentration was also observed only in fibers < 1 hr after exercise (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by fura-2 measurements of resting Ca2+ shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both total releasable Ca2+ store content and myoplasmic resting Ca2+ concentration were increased significantly after 10 stimulus trains in fibers from mice < 1 hr after exercise compared to fibers from control mice and mice < 1 hr after exercise in the absence of stimulation.
source: Importantly, both total releasable Ca2+ store content and myoplasmic resting Ca2+ concentration were increased significantly after 10 stimulus trains in fibers from mice < 1 hr after exercise compared to that observed for fibers from both control mice and mice < 1 hr after exercise in the absence of stimulation (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: This is supported by fura-FF and fura-2 measurements shown in Figures 5D and 5E.

claim: Resting free Ca2+ concentration in the SR lumen was not altered in FDB fibers from mice < 1 hr after exercise.
source: In contrast, resting free Ca2+ concentration in the SR lumen (Figure 5—figure supplement 2) was not altered in FDB fibers from mice < 1 hr after exercise.
evidence: This is supported by D1ER measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: No difference in either the amplitudes or time constants of twitch Ca2+ transient decay were observed after delivery of 10 consecutive, high-frequency stimulus trains in FDB fibers isolated from either sedentary mice or <1 hr after exercise.
source: No difference in either the amplitudes or time constants of twitch Ca2+ transient decay were observed after delivery of 10 consecutive, high-frequency stimulus trains (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B–D) in FDB fibers isolated from either sedentary mice or <1 hr after exercise.
evidence: This is supported by kinetic analysis of twitch Ca2+ transient decay shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Average force-frequency curves and peak tetanic-specific force were not significantly different across all four conditions (control, <1 hr, 6 hr, and 24 hr after exercise).
source: Average force-frequency curves and peak tetanic-specific force were not significantly different across all four conditions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by force-frequency measurements shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: All experimental conditions exhibited a similar modest reduction in peak force during the 2nd stimulus train, followed by a rebound increase (bump-phase) that generally lasted ~10–12 stimulus trains.
source: All experimental conditions exhibited a similar modest reduction in peak force during the 2nd stimulus train, followed by a rebound increase (referred to as the bump-phase) that generally lasted ~10–12 stimulus trains (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by force measurements during repetitive stimulation shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: The peak-specific force generated during the first stimulus train was not different between the four conditions.
source: While the peak-specific force generated during the first stimulus train was not different between the four conditions (Figure 6A, left)
evidence: This is supported by force measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Maximal specific force increased significantly during stimulus trains 7–30 in EDL muscles from mice < 1 hr after exercise.
source: While the peak-specific force generated during the first stimulus train was not different between the four conditions (Figure 6A, left), maximal specific force increased significantly during stimulus trains 7–30 in EDL muscles from mice < 1 hr after exercise (Figure 6A, middle)
evidence: This is supported by force measurements shown in Figure 6A and quantified in Figure 6B.

claim: The potentiation of force in EDL muscles from mice < 1 hr after exercise was lost by the end of the repetitive stimulation protocol.
source: While the peak-specific force generated during the first stimulus train was not different between the four conditions (Figure 6A, left), maximal specific force increased significantly during stimulus trains 7–30 in EDL muscles from mice < 1 hr after exercise (Figure 6A, middle), a potentiation that was lost by the end of the protocol (Figure 6A, right).
evidence: This is supported by force measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Both peak-specific force and the maximum magnitude of the bump-phase were increased 20–25% in EDL muscles from mice < 1 hr after exercise.
source: As a result, both peak-specific force (Figure 6D) and the maximum magnitude of the bump-phase (Figure 6E) were increased 20–25%.
evidence: This is supported by force measurements shown in Figures 6D and 6E.

claim: SOCE induced by pharmacological SR Ca2+ depletion was absent in FDB fibers isolated from iOrai1 KO mice.
source: Consistent with that reported previously (Carrell et al., 2016), SOCE induced by pharmacological SR Ca2+ depletion was absent in FDB fibers isolated from iOrai1 KO mice (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is supported by Mn2+ quench measurements shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: FDB fibers from iOrai1 KO mice < 1 hr after exercise lacked detectable Mn2+ quench following pharmacological store depletion.
source: Similarly, FDB fibers from iOrai1 KO mice < 1 hr after exercise also lacked detectable Mn2+ quench following pharmacological store depletion (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: This is supported by Mn2+ quench measurements shown in Figures 7A and 7B.

claim: Constitutive SOCE in the absence of store depletion was absent in fibers isolated from both control iOrai1 KO mice and iOrai1 KO mice < 1 hr after exercise.
source: In addition, constitutive SOCE in the absence of store depletion (-depletion), was also absent in fibers isolated from both control iOrai1 KO mice and iOrai1 KO mice < 1 hr after exercise (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: This is supported by Mn2+ quench measurements shown in Figures 7C and 7D.

claim: The bump-phase of muscle contraction during repetitive stimulation was suppressed in EDL muscles from control iOrai1 KO mice.
source: Finally, the bump-phase of muscle contraction during repetitive stimulation was suppressed in EDL muscles from control iOrai1 KO mice and was not further enhanced <1 hr after exercise (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This is supported by force measurements shown in Figures 7E and 7F.

claim: The bump-phase of muscle contraction during repetitive stimulation was not enhanced <1 hr after exercise in EDL muscles from iOrai1 KO mice.
source: Finally, the bump-phase of muscle contraction during repetitive stimulation was suppressed in EDL muscles from control iOrai1 KO mice and was not further enhanced <1 hr after exercise (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This is supported by force measurements shown in Figures 7E and 7F.

claim: Similar results to iOrai1 KO mice were obtained in dnOrai1 mice, which also specifically lack SOCE in skeletal muscle.
source: Similar results were obtained in dnOrai1 mice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), which also specifically lack SOCE in skeletal muscle (Wei-Lapierre et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous characterization of dnOrai1 mice.

claim: CEUs are dynamic structures that assemble during exercise and disassemble following recovery.
source: The results, summarized in the model shown in Figure 8, demonstrate that: a) CEUs are dynamic structures that assemble during exercise and disassemble following recovery (Figures 1 and 2)
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the time course data for SR-stacks and TT extensions shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: TT retraction from the I band following exercise occurs before SR-stack disassembly.
source: The results, summarized in the model shown in Figure 8, demonstrate that: a) CEUs are dynamic structures that assemble during exercise and disassemble following recovery (Figures 1 and 2); b) TT retraction from the I band following exercise occurs before SR-stack disassembly (Figures 1 and 2)
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the different time courses for TT retraction and SR-stack disassembly shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Peak SOCE activity, reduced Ca2+ store content and increased resting Ca2+, as well as sustained Ca2+ transient amplitude and force production during repetitive stimulation all increase/decrease in parallel with the time course of TT extension within the I band.
source: The results, summarized in the model shown in Figure 8, demonstrate that: a) CEUs are dynamic structures that assemble during exercise and disassemble following recovery (Figures 1 and 2); b) TT retraction from the I band following exercise occurs before SR-stack disassembly (Figures 1 and 2); c) peak SOCE activity (i.e. maximum rate of Mn2+ quench), reduced Ca2+ store content and increased resting Ca2+, as well as sustained Ca2+ transient amplitude and force production during repetitive stimulation all increase/decrease in parallel with the time course of TT extension within the I band (Figures 3, 5 and 6)
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the parallel time courses observed in Figures 3, 5, and 6.

claim: Exercise-induced CEU formation results in constitutively-activated SOCE.
source: The results, summarized in the model shown in Figure 8, demonstrate that: a) CEUs are dynamic structures that assemble during exercise and disassemble following recovery (Figures 1 and 2); b) TT retraction from the I band following exercise occurs before SR-stack disassembly (Figures 1 and 2); c) peak SOCE activity (i.e. maximum rate of Mn2+ quench), reduced Ca2+ store content and increased resting Ca2+, as well as sustained Ca2+ transient amplitude and force production during repetitive stimulation all increase/decrease in parallel with the time course of TT extension within the I band (Figures 3, 5 and 6); d) exercise-induced CEU formation results in constitutively-activated SOCE (Figure 4)
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the constitutive Mn2+ quench observed in Figure 4.

claim: Increased SOCE activity and sustained force production during repetitive stimulation requires Orai1 channels.
source: The results, summarized in the model shown in Figure 8, demonstrate that: a) CEUs are dynamic structures that assemble during exercise and disassemble following recovery (Figures 1 and 2); b) TT retraction from the I band following exercise occurs before SR-stack disassembly (Figures 1 and 2); c) peak SOCE activity (i.e. maximum rate of Mn2+ quench), reduced Ca2+ store content and increased resting Ca2+, as well as sustained Ca2+ transient amplitude and force production during repetitive stimulation all increase/decrease in parallel with the time course of TT extension within the I band (Figures 3, 5 and 6); d) exercise-induced CEU formation results in constitutively-activated SOCE (Figure 4); and e) increased SOCE activity and sustained force production during repetitive stimulation requires Orai1 channels (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the loss of exercise-induced functional benefits in Orai1-deficient mice shown in Figure 7.

claim: The stacks of flat-parallel SR cisternae formed after exercise are functionally competent CEUs only when associated with a TT extended from the triad.
source: Together, these results indicate that the stacks of flat-parallel SR cisternae formed after exercise are functionally competent CEUs only when associated with a TT extended from the triad.
evidence: This is an integrative conclusion based on the observation that functional effects parallel TT extension rather than SR-stack persistence.

claim: TTs retract from the CEU following exercise prior to SR-stack disassembly.
source: Two main findings of this study are: a) TTs retract from the CEU following exercise prior to SR-stack disassembly (Figures 1 and 2)
evidence: This is a main finding based on the different time courses shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Exercise-dependent increases in Orai1-mediated SOCE, intracellular Ca2+ dynamics, and maintained contractile activity during repetitive stimulation decline with a time course like that of TT retraction.
source: Two main findings of this study are: a) TTs retract from the CEU following exercise prior to SR-stack disassembly (Figures 1 and 2) and b) exercise-dependent increases in Orai1-mediated SOCE (Figures 3, 4 and 7), intracellular Ca2+ dynamics (Figure 5), and maintained contractile activity during repetitive stimulation (Figure 6) declines with a time course like that of TT retraction.
evidence: This is a main finding based on the parallel time courses of TT retraction and functional changes.

claim: The functional effects of acute exercise are controlled by association of TTs (containing Orai1 proteins) with SR-stacks (containing STIM1 proteins) in the I band.
source: Together, these results show that the functional effects of acute exercise are controlled by association of TTs (containing Orai1 proteins) with SR-stacks (containing STIM1 proteins) in the I band, with an increase of TT/SR contact length that provides a greater surface area for STIM1-Orai1 interaction.
evidence: This is an integrative conclusion based on the correlation between TT-SR contact and functional outcomes.

claim: An increase of TT/SR contact length provides a greater surface area for STIM1-Orai1 interaction.
source: Together, these results show that the functional effects of acute exercise are controlled by association of TTs (containing Orai1 proteins) with SR-stacks (containing STIM1 proteins) in the I band, with an increase of TT/SR contact length that provides a greater surface area for STIM1-Orai1 interaction.
evidence: This is a mechanistic inference based on the structural observations.

claim: Both ER-ER contacts in non-muscle cells overexpressing STIM1 and SR-SR contacts in muscle after acute exercise exhibit small electron dense bridges within a similar junctional gap width (~8 nm).
source: Interestingly, both ER-ER contacts in non-muscle cells overexpressing STIM1 and SR-SR contacts in muscle after acute exercise exhibit small electron dense bridges within a similar junctional gap width (~8 nm).
evidence: This is based on comparison with cited studies on STIM1 overexpression in non-muscle cells.

claim: The small electron dense bridges observed in EM images likely reflect STIM1 proteins.
source: These similarities in membrane structure and gap width are consistent with the small electron dense bridges observed in EM images reflecting STIM1 proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity to structures in STIM1-overexpressing cells.

claim: STIM1-containing SR-stacks could be needed to efficiently trap Orai1 channels during TT elongation into the I band.
source: Similar to the 'diffusion trap' model of STIM1-Orai1 coupling in non-excitable cells proposed previously (Wu et al., 2014), one possible interpretation of these findings is that STIM1-containing SR-stacks could be needed to efficiently trap Orai1 channels during TT elongation into the I band.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on analogy to the diffusion trap model in non-muscle cells.

claim: The constitutive Ca2+ entry observed <1 hr after exercise is unlikely to represent increased susceptibility of fibers to damage shortly after exercise.
source: As the constitutive Ca2+ entry in these fibers was rapidly blocked by application of BTP-2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), the constitutive entry in these fibers is unlikely to represent increased susceptibility of fibers to damage shortly after exercise.
evidence: This is an inference based on the BTP-2 sensitivity of the constitutive entry.

claim: The constitutive Ca2+ entry is mediated by Orai1 channels rather than TrpC or mechano-sensitive channels.
source: In support of this idea, the constitutive Ca2+ entry observed <1 hr after exercise is absent in fibers from two separate mouse models deficient in Orai1 function (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1). These findings suggest that the constitutive Ca2+ entry is mediated by Orai1 channels (rather than TrpC or mechano-sensitive channels).
evidence: This is an inference based on the loss of constitutive entry in Orai1-deficient mice.

claim: The majority of the D1ER signal originated from the triad junction.
source: It is important to note, however, that D1ER localization studies indicate that the majority of the D1ER signal originated from the triad junction (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence localization studies shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The D1ER measurements suggest that the free Ca2+ concentration within the triad junction is not different after exercise.
source: Thus, the D1ER measurements suggest that the free Ca2+ concentration within the triad junction is not different after exercise.
evidence: This is an inference based on the D1ER measurements and localization.

claim: Constitutive Ca2+ entry observed after exercise most likely does not originate from Orai1 channels within the triad junction.
source: Thus, constitutive Ca2+ entry observed after exercise most likely does not originate from Orai1 channels within the triad junction.
evidence: This is an inference based on the D1ER measurements showing no change in triad SR Ca2+.

claim: Constitutive entry may arise from Orai1 channels in CEUs assembled during exercise in the I band region of the sarcomere.
source: Rather, constitutive entry may arise from Orai1 channels in another location, possibly CEUs assembled during exercise in the I band region of the sarcomere that are not well-reflected in the spatially-averaged D1ER signal.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural and functional data.

claim: Exercise could produce a signal that directly activates Orai1 independent of store depletion.
source: An alternative explanation is that exercise could produce a signal that directly activates Orai1 independent of store depletion.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for constitutive SOCE.

claim: The increase in constitutive Ca2+ entry observed <1 hr after exercise could explain the elevation in resting Ca2+ concentration observed at this time point.
source: Assuming no changes in the properties of sarcolemmal Ca2+ efflux mechanisms, the increase in constitutive Ca2+ entry observed <1 hr after exercise could explain the elevation in resting Ca2+ concentration observed at this time point (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between constitutive entry and elevated resting Ca2+.

claim: Partial Ca2+ depletion within SR-stacks of the CEU represents one possible mechanism for the constitutive entry observed immediately following exercise.
source: Again, partial Ca2+ depletion within SR-stacks of the CEU represents one possible mechanism for the constitutive entry observed immediately following exercise.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for constitutive SOCE.

claim: The constitutive Ca2+ entry observed after exercise could reflect Stim2-mediated activation of Orai1 channels within the CEUs.
source: Alternatively, as lower levels of store depletion are sufficient for Stim2 to activate Orai1-dependent Ca2+ entry (Brandman et al., 2007; Thiel et al., 2013), the constitutive Ca2+ entry observed after exercise could reflect Stim2-mediated activation of Orai1 channels within the CEUs.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative mechanism based on known properties of Stim2.

claim: CEUs may reflect the subcellular location for the constitutive SOCE observed <1 hr after exercise.
source: One possibility is that, as proposed above, CEUs may reflect the subcellular location for the constitutive SOCE observed <1 hr after exercise.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Pre-existing STIM and Orai1 complexes distinct from newly formed CEUs could also contribute to the observed increase in SOCE function.
source: However, given that total releasable Ca2+ store content at rest was reduced <1 hr after exercise, it is possible that pre-existing STIM and Orai1 complexes distinct from newly formed CEUs could also contribute to the observed increase in SOCE function.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the non-linear relationship between structure and function.

claim: The observed increase in peak Ca2+ transient amplitude after acute exercise results, at least in part, from enhanced SOCE activity promoting SR refilling and total releasable Ca2+ content to a level sufficient to augment Ca2+ flux.
source: Together, these findings are consistent with the observed increase in peak Ca2+ transient amplitude (and force production) after acute exercise resulting, at least in part, from enhanced SOCE activity promoting SR refilling and total releasable Ca2+ content to a level sufficient to augment Ca2+ flux.
evidence: This is an integrative conclusion based on the Ca2+ store content and transient amplitude data.

claim: The bump-phase of the repetitive stimulation contraction curve reflects the contribution of Orai1-dependent SOCE.
source: The following observations are consistent with this bump-phase reflecting the contribution of Orai1-dependent SOCE: 1) it is reduced by interventions (BTP-2, 2-APB, 0 Ca2+) that reduce SOCE (Boncompagni et al., 2017); 2) it is increased <1 hr after treadmill exercise when SOCE is also increased; 3) it is unaltered 6 and 24 hr after treadmill exercise when SOCE activity has returned to control levels; 4) it is absent in mice lacking Orai1-dependent Ca2+ entry both under control conditions and after acute exercise.
evidence: This is an inference based on multiple lines of evidence including pharmacological inhibition, time course correlation, and genetic deletion.

claim: CEUs formed after acute exercise represent an adaptive response of skeletal muscle to exercise that augments Orai1-dependent Ca2+ entry to optimize myoplasmic Ca2+ dynamics in a manner that limits muscle force decline during sustained activation.
source: In conclusion, the findings reported here support the idea that CEUs formed after acute exercise represent an adaptive response of skeletal muscle to exercise that augments Orai1-dependent Ca2+ entry to optimize myoplasmic Ca2+ dynamics in a manner that limits muscle force decline during sustained activation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, integrating all the findings.
